solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: see 14dn.
(& 26dn.) Be prepared to shoot said exposed members!

indicators.note: what is said reaches the ear as sound alone, so the spelling written down need not be the spelling heard

blocks.note: members are limbs, and limbs with nothing on them are bare — spoken aloud, that is what goes in the grid

explanation.surface: A shout about people standing around with their sleeves rolled up while a gun is readied.
explanation.walkthrough: The right to bear arms is the American constitutional phrase, and the clue hears skin where the phrase means weapons. 'Members' is the old word for limbs, which is what lets arms be both.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear arms is to carry weapons, and anyone carrying them is by definition prepared to shoot.

clue.text: Cat round church by chance

blocks.note: a round thing drawn on paper is the letter O
ce = Church of England, the crossword's default church
your lot is what chance deals you, as in casting lots

explanation.surface: Somebody happens upon a cat circling a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat round church' reads as one picture, so the eye takes 'round' for a preposition when it is standing in for a letter. Only the first word of the clue is definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocelot is the spotted wildcat of Central and South America, so the bare word 'cat' covers it by example.

clue.text: Multinational's reluctant role brings stress on settler

definitions.note: The answer names the part played rather than the abstract word 'role'; a multinational's reluctant role is that of taxpayer, and the possessive carries the shorthand.

indicators.note: in a down entry one thing sits on another by being written above it, so the piece named first takes the top

blocks.note: to tax someone's patience is to put it under stress
the one who settles the bill is the one who pays

explanation.surface: A multinational is stuck with a job it never wanted, and it piles pressure on a settler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settler' poses as a colonist and means whoever settles up — the same verb as settling a bill. The target is the company that pays its tax only under protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that routes its profits elsewhere is still a taxpayer, and grudgingly is the only way it plays the part.

clue.text: Lovers finally come together, rising up, and hum

indicators.note: 'finally' points at the end of the word in front of it, the letter that word finishes on
in a down clue what rises is read from the bottom of the grid upwards, against the order given

blocks.note: the last letter of loverS
to knit is to come together, and KNIT read up the grid gives these four

explanation.surface: Two lovers at last come together, rising up, and hum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hum' is British slang for a bad smell — the sense in 'this place hums'. The lovers are there to sell the picture, and only their last letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a thing that hums smells foul, which is exactly what a thing that stinks does.

clue.text: One who'd broadcast?  You bet!

indicators.note: seed broadcast over a field lands scattered, and scattered letters keep no order

blocks.note: 'one' is the article AN, and WHO'D supplies the other four letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks who on earth would put such a thing on the air, and gets an emphatic answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is doing its farming job — seed thrown wide — rather than its radio one, and the radio sense is the whole of the misdirection. The answer is the emphatic agreement of a 1940s film.
explanation.definitionFit: 'And how!' is the exclamation that agrees hard with what has just been said, which is the job 'You bet!' does.

clue.text: America: scrap number one's ascent – object!

indicators.note: something in ascent is climbing, and in a down clue a climbing word is read from its foot upwards

blocks.note: am = America, the standard short form
a scrap of something is a bit of it
number is No. and one is I; NOI climbing the grid reads as these three

explanation.surface: America is told to abandon its climb to the top spot, and somebody protests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object!' with its exclamation mark begs to be heard as the verb, and it is the noun — an aim. No. for number is the abbreviation on an invoice, and I is the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: Your object is the thing you have set yourself to reach, the aim sense of the word rather than the thing you can pick up.

clue.text: Endless, crap, odd cereal produce

indicators.note: a word described as endless has had its end taken off, so its final letter never appears

blocks.note: a crap thing is a dud, and DUD with no end left is DU
rum is the old word for odd or peculiar, as in 'a rum do'

explanation.surface: A sour verdict on a crop: it goes on forever, it is rubbish, and it is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' for odd is Victorian slang kept alive by crosswords and by 'a rum do'. Three complaints in a row read as one opinion, which is what hides the join between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Durum is the hard wheat grown for semolina and pasta flour, so it is cereal produce in the farmer's sense.

clue.text: Trafficker's car hits hard worker

blocks.note: a Merc is a Mercedes, British shorthand for the car
h = hard, the grade stamped on a pencil
the worker ant, the crossword's standard labourer

explanation.surface: A dealer's Mercedes runs into a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: The collision is entirely surface: nothing strikes anything, the pieces merely stand next to each other. 'Merchant' keeps the old wide sense of anyone who deals in something.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant deals in goods, and a trafficker is a dealer too — the word stretches across the respectable trade and the shady one.

clue.text: Lawyer's deal to protect Republican lives

indicators.note: you protect a thing by standing all the way round it, so one word closes over another

blocks.note: to barter is to deal, and the word opens up to let something inside
r = Republican, the letter beside a candidate's name on a US ballot
'he lives' and 'he is' take the same verb, so lives = is

explanation.surface: A lawyer's deal is shielding a Republican for as long as he lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives' for IS is worth filing away: swap the verb into 'he is' and the two letters fall out. The deal is barter rather than a plea bargain, which is the other half of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrister is the lawyer who argues the case in court, the wigged half of the British profession as against the solicitor.

clue.text: Liberal senator's duplicity

indicators.note: a liberal helping is a loose one, and letters treated loosely will not stay where they were put

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A Liberal senator turns out to have been playing both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L offers a party where the setter means 'loose', and a Liberal senator is a plausible enough creature to keep the disguise standing. The whole answer sits inside one word of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name betrayal from within: duplicity is playing both sides, and treason is that done to your own country.

clue.text: Nothing regressive about having an erection, flower!

indicators.note: to regress is to go back the way you came, so those letters are read backwards
what is placed about a thing is wrapped round the outside of it

blocks.note: nothing is nil, and NIL turned back to front gives LIN
what is erect is up

explanation.surface: Nobody is bothered in the slightest about a man having an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops keeps the smut in the wordplay and leaves the definition honest, so the last word of the clue is the one to trust. NIL is the piece that does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: The lupin is the tall garden spike of pea-like blooms, so 'flower' names it by example.

clue.text: Times: "Europe's top politician in sex U-turn"

indicators.note: the top of a word is where it begins, so the letter it starts with is the one taken
what is in something sits inside it, with that thing's letters closing on either side
a U-turn sends you back along the road you came by, so those letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: 'it' is the old euphemism for sex, and IT after its U-turn reads TI
the first letter of Europe
an MP is a Member of Parliament, the crossword's default politician

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline has Europe's leading politician changing his mind about sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' opens the clue like a masthead and means speeds instead — tempo is Italian, and its plural keeps the Italian ending. 'It' for sex is old slang that crosswords have kept in circulation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempi are the speeds a piece of music is taken at, and time in that musical sense is what the plural counts.

clue.text: Fellow feeling English premier all over at Hungary's borders

indicators.note: turned all over means flipped end for end, so those letters come out the other way round
a country's borders are its outer edges, so the first and last letters are the ones wanted

blocks.note: e = English, the usual single letter
the premier is the PM, and PM turned over reads MP
the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands
the outer letters of Hungary

explanation.surface: An English prime minister is all over the place at the Hungarian border.
explanation.walkthrough: PM and MP are the same pair of letters either way round, which is the only reason 'all over' has to be in the clue at all. Hungary is there for its H and its Y, not its politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow feeling is the old phrase for sharing what someone else is going through, which is what empathy names.

clue.text: (& 1dn.) "Collapsing? Pity," I snapped, being a devious minister?

definitions.note: A devious minister is not the same thing as the activity named; the question mark admits the stretch, defining the answer by what such a minister spends his day doing.

indicators.note: something snapped has broken, and once broken the pieces can go back together any way at all

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters across the two entries

explanation.surface: Somebody snaps back sarcastically that it is a great pity the thing should be falling down.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the opening words look like speech to be read when they are letters to be rearranged. Fifteen letters spread over two entries is about as long as an anagram comes.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister who plays politics is working the angles for his own side instead of governing, which is where the deviousness lies.

clue.text: Elected at cost, being the leader

blocks.note: a candidate who wins is in, the way a party is in power
the charge for a thing is what it costs you

explanation.surface: Winning the election came at a price for the new leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary words doing ordinary jobs, so the only work is seeing 'elected' as the two letters of 'in power'. A charge is equally a fee, an accusation and an attack, and the fee is the sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever is in charge holds the authority rather than the title, which is what leading a thing amounts to.

clue.text: People come to have them almost mow grass badly

indicators.note: almost a whole word is all of it but the last letter, which never arrives
a job done badly comes out wrong, and letters in the wrong order are exactly that

blocks.note: MOW stopped one letter short of the end
the rest of the fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: People turn up to give the grass a half-hearted and thoroughly bad mowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come' is the hinge of the clue: the innocent coming round of the surface against the other sense the definition leans on. The mowing is there only to hand over letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming is the plain verb for having one, so the definition describes the answer by what people are said to do when they get there.

clue.text: Troublemakers' smirks about email "lacking modern technology"

indicators.note: one thing set about another goes all the way round the outside of it
what a thing lacks is missing from it, so those letters are struck out before the rest is used

blocks.note: a smirk is a grin, and this one opens up to take something inside
AI is artificial intelligence, the modern technology of the hour
EMAIL with its AI taken away

explanation.surface: Someone's smirking messages about a firm still stuck in the technological dark ages.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters removed are themselves clued, by a phrase that looks like plain office grumbling. Gremlins were invented by RAF crews in the 1940s as the imps that sabotage aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A gremlin is the mischievous imp blamed when machinery plays up, so gremlins are troublemakers by trade.

clue.text: It might stop clots working in Paris

indicators.note: dough that is worked is pushed about until it takes a new shape, and letters get the same treatment

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Something is going to stop a set of idiots getting any work done in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' nearly always asks for a word to be put into French, and here it is only seven letters to shuffle. A clot is a fool as well as a lump in the blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirin thins the blood, which is why a daily low dose is prescribed to stop clots forming.

clue.text: House possibly gets peer to restrain unruly toper

indicators.note: to restrain someone is to hold them from every side, so one piece shuts round another
an unruly crowd will not keep its lines, and unruly letters will not keep their order

blocks.note: to peer into someone's business is to pry
the five letters of TOPER in a new order; a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A lord takes hold of a rowdy drunk before any damage is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' has just conjured the Lords, so 'peer' arrives looking like a man in ermine when it is the verb for prying. A toper is an old word for a soak.
explanation.definitionFit: A house is one kind of property, the estate agent's word covering everything from a flat to a field — which is what 'possibly' concedes.

clue.text: "F**k off Enid!" is a respectful form of address?

indicators.note: food that has gone off has turned, and a word that has turned no longer holds its letters in place

blocks.note: to eff is the printable form of the verb, as in effing and blinding
the four letters of ENID rearranged

explanation.surface: Somebody is bawling at poor Enid to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: The asterisks are a word in their own right: what you say when you are not saying the other one. The question mark marks the distance between the shout and the courtesy it spells.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi is the Turkish title of respect for a man of standing, the Ottoman world's equivalent of 'sir'.

clue.text: Agent works butt off

indicators.note: the butt is the blunt back end of a thing, and taking it off costs the word its last letter

blocks.note: a works is a factory, as in the gasworks

explanation.surface: An agent puts in a long day and works his backside off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' is the noun, a plant with a chimney, rather than the verb the surface hands you, and 'butt' is the blunt end before it is anybody's backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A factor is an agent who acts for another — in Scotland, the man who runs an estate on the landowner's behalf.

clue.text: Sex appeal makes balls and member hot

blocks.note: two balls drawn on the page are two Os
mp = Member of Parliament
h = hot, the letter on the tap

explanation.surface: The recipe for animal magnetism: balls, plus one overheated Member of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'balls' and 'member' are chosen to sound crude while doing perfectly straight crossword jobs. Oomph has meant magnetism since the 1930s, when Ann Sheridan was billed as the Oomph Girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is the vigour that turns heads, and sex appeal is the particular kind of it the word was coined to name.

clue.text: State's working for builder

blocks.note: ma = Massachusetts, and the clue's own apostrophe-s hands over its letter
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: The state is doing its bit for the building trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is not punctuation here but a letter, which is why the state can be had in two. MA is the postal abbreviation for Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: A mason builds in stone, the trade the word named for centuries before the lodges borrowed it.

clue.text: Main film's glib?

blocks.note: the skin of oil lying on open water
too smooth by half, the way a salesman talks

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the big feature film is all surface and no substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the old noun for the open sea, the one preserved in the Spanish Main, so the film in question is floating on salt water rather than showing at the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: A slick is the film of oil spread across the main, and a slick talker is the glib one who is too smooth to be trusted.

clue.text: Colour of little shrunken Bill

indicators.note: a shrunken word is the word written small, in the clipped form a nickname uses

blocks.note: little cut down to lil, the way Lilian becomes Lil
a/c is the account, the bill a firm sends out

explanation.surface: A small man named Bill, shrunk smaller still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' is the invoice, not the man the capital letter offers, and a/c is how a ledger writes account. Nothing in the clue is doing the job its surface claims.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac is the pale mauve of the shrub's blossom, a colour named straight off the plant that bears it.

clue.text: Putin's role: to arouse gross rage

definitions.note: The answer names the part played rather than the abstract word 'role', a shorthand the possessive carries.

indicators.note: to arouse a thing is to stir it up, and stirred letters settle in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Putin's part in the business is to whip up an ugly fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arouse' is the instruction rather than part of the picture — what it stirs is nine letters, not a mood. Cyclops habitually writes his opinion of the target into the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The aggressor is the one who starts the fight rather than the one answering it, and that is the part the clue casts.

clue.text: see 2dn.
Party battle for a starter?

blocks.note: Con is the Conservatives as a ballot paper prints them
the Somme, the 1916 battle on the Western Front

explanation.surface: A brawl at a party, served up before anyone reaches the main course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' promises a celebration and delivers the Conservatives, which is the one switch the clue asks of you. The question mark covers consommé being only one starter among many.
explanation.definitionFit: Consommé is the clear soup that opens a meal, so 'a starter' defines it by example.

clue.text: Leaders of several countries easily got round Brown's position

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, the one it starts from
to get round a thing is to go the whole way about it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words in turn
tan is a shade of brown

explanation.surface: The heads of several countries talked their way round Brown's position without much trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' has to be read twice over — heads of government in the surface, opening letters in the wordplay. Gordon Brown was the British prime minister the capital letter is nudging you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: A stance is the position you take on a question, the figurative use of the word for how a person stands.
